title: Jacob Blesses Joseph's Two Sons
overview: Near death, Jacob adopts Joseph's two sons born in Egypt as his own and blesses them, deliberately giving the younger one the greater blessing.

parts.label: Joseph visits his dying father (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Joseph hears Jacob is ill and brings his two sons so they can receive their grandfather's blessing. The old man gathers his strength and sits up to receive them.

parts.label: Jacob adopts the two boys (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: Jacob recalls God's promise at Luz (also called Bethel) of many descendants and the land of Canaan, then claims Joseph's sons as his own, equal to his oldest sons Reuben and Simeon. This gives Joseph a double share, since each boy later becomes a full tribe of Israel; the brief mention of Rachel, Joseph's mother, may hint at why, though the text does not say so.

parts.label: Meeting the grandsons (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Jacob, nearly blind, kisses and holds the boys, amazed that he lived to see Joseph again and his children too. Joseph bows low, showing respect before the formal blessing begins.

parts.label: The crossed hands (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Joseph places the firstborn Manasseh by Jacob's right hand, the hand of greater honor, but Jacob crosses his arms on purpose to put it on the younger Ephraim. He then asks the God who shepherded him all his life, and the angel who rescued him from every harm, to bless the boys; Christians have often read this angel as a glimpse of Christ.

parts.label: Joseph objects (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: Joseph tries to move his father's hand, but Jacob insists, echoing a pattern in Genesis where the younger is chosen over the older, and Ephraim did later become the leading tribe of the northern kingdom. Jewish parents still bless their sons with the words of verse 20.

parts.label: Last words and a gift (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: Jacob assures Joseph that God will bring the family back to Canaan and gives him an extra portion of land; the Hebrew word for this portion sounds like Shechem, a town Joseph's descendants later held. No earlier story tells of Jacob taking land there by sword, so scholars are unsure what event he means.

think: When someone deliberately breaks the expected order of things, like giving the younger child the bigger blessing, when does that feel like wisdom and when does it feel like unfairness?
